t.1.138.2: He, crushing the great trees that were in flower and those bearing fruit, and breaking the woody thickets that grew near his path, went on.
t.1.138.1: As he strode swiftly onward, O king, a wind blew, stirred up by the force of his thighs, like the wind that rises at the coming of the hot months Śuci and Śukra.
t.1.138.3: Thus he of boundless prowess went on, breaking the trees as he went; from the force of his speed something like a swoon came over the sons of Pāṇḍu.
t.1.138.4: Again and again, crossing waters whose far shores lay distant by swimming with their arms, they then kept to the road in concealment, out of fear of the Dhārtarāṣṭras.
t.1.138.6: In the evening those bulls of the Bharatas came to a region of the forest that was terrible, scant in roots, fruits and water, and full of fierce birds and beasts.
t.1.138.5: There, over rough and uneven riverbanks, he carried his mother alone on his back with difficulty, that delicate and illustrious lady.
t.1.138.7: The twilight became dreadful, the beasts and birds were fierce, and all the quarters were darkened by unseasonable winds.
t.1.138.8: Those Kauravyas, oppressed by weariness and by thirst, and by sleep that had grown strong upon them, were then unable to go on.
t.1.138.9: Then Bhīma, having entered the vast, terrible, and desolate forest, hastened to a lovely banyan tree with wide-spreading shade.
t.1.138.10: Having set them all down there, the bull among the Bharatas said, "I will look for water here; rest yourselves," O lord.
t.1.138.11: These sārasa cranes, creatures that move upon the water, are crying sweetly; surely there is a great body of water here, such is my thought.
t.1.138.12: Permitted by his eldest brother with the words "Go," O Bhārata, he went to the place where the water-dwelling creatures were crying out.
t.1.138.13: Having drunk the water there and bathed, O bull among the Bharatas, he then brought back water in his upper garment, O king.
t.1.138.14: Having come back in haste from a distance of a gavyūti toward his mother, Vṛkodara saw his mother and his brothers asleep on the bare ground, and, his heart overwhelmed with grief, he lamented bitterly.
t.1.138.15: Those who once, in Vāraṇāvata, could not find sleep even on the most costly beds now lie asleep upon the bare ground.
t.1.138.16: Kuntī, the sister of Vasudeva, crusher of hosts of enemies, the daughter of Kuntibhoja, honored for bearing every auspicious mark.
t.1.138.18: Behold her today, the most delicate of women, accustomed to costly beds, lying here upon the bare ground, which she has never known.
t.1.138.17: The daughter-in-law of Vicitravīrya, the wife of the great-souled Pāṇḍu, she who always slept in palaces, whose radiance was like the inner petals of a lotus.
t.1.138.19: She who bore these sons from Dharma, from Indra and from Vāyu, she herself, utterly wearied, now lies upon the bare ground, unaccustomed to such a thing.
t.1.138.20: What could I possibly see that is more painful than this, I who today see these tigers among men lying asleep upon the bare ground?
t.1.138.21: The king, knower of dharma, who deserves sovereignty over the three worlds, how is it that he now lies exhausted on the bare ground like a common man?
t.1.138.22: This one, dark as a blue rain-cloud, unequalled among men on earth, lies upon the ground like a common man; what could be more painful than this?
t.1.138.23: These two, who in the splendor of their beauty are like the Aśvins among the gods, now lie asleep today upon the bare ground like common men.
t.1.138.24: He who has no hostile kinsmen, defilers of the family, may live very happily in the world, like a tree standing alone in a village.
t.1.138.26: Those who have many valiant kinsmen devoted to dharma live happily in the world and remain free from harm.
t.1.138.25: For a single tree in a village that is laden with leaves and fruit, standing without kin, becomes a sacred caitya tree, worthy of reverence and richly worshipped.
t.1.138.27: Strong, prosperous in their aims, and delighting their friends and kinsmen, they live by depending on one another, like trees born in the forest.
t.1.138.29: Freed from that fire, we have taken refuge at this tree; having met with the most extreme hardship, which direction shall we take?
t.1.138.28: But we have been banished by the evil-minded Dhṛtarāṣṭra together with his son, at his command, and somehow we were not burned.
t.1.138.30: For I perceive a city not very far from this forest. When they ought to be keeping watch, these men sleep; well then, I myself will keep watch.
t.1.138.31: "These will drink the water later, when they have woken up with their weariness overcome." Having resolved thus, Bhīma himself then stayed awake.
